_comment: R-124 deletion-journal bucket policy TEMPLATE. Replace every <PLACEHOLDER>.
Applied by an operator with `aws s3api put-bucket-policy`; the application
never creates, reads or applies this.
THIS IS THE POLICY THAT IS ACTUALLY DEPLOYED. It was regenerated on
2026-09-08 from the rendered document applied to the live bucket, whose
sha256 is recorded in RUNBOOK.md. Strip this _comment before submitting to
AWS -- a top-level _comment is not valid in a policy document.
THREE CORRECTIONS LIVE PROVISIONING FOUND, none of which any test in this
repository could have caught (see POLICY-CHANGES.md):
* s3:x-amz-object-lock-mode WAS INVALID. The correct key is
s3:object-lock-mode -- the x-amz- prefix belongs to the encryption and
ACL keys, not to Object Lock. AWS Access Analyzer reported
INVALID_SERVICE_CONDITION_KEY, which means DenyWeakOrAbsentObjectLock
never evaluated as intended and the writer condition never matched.
* The tampering denial can NOT include s3:PutObjectRetention: a blanket
non-break-glass denial of it also denies the retention authorization
every valid upload needs. Shorter-than-28-day and non-COMPLIANCE
retention are still denied, by the two statements above it.
* s3:PutBucketObjectLockConfiguration and s3:PutEncryptionConfiguration
were missing from the tampering denial, so the bucket's actual default
retention and default encryption were unprotected.
Condition keys otherwise verified 2026-09-08 against the AWS docs:
DenyNonConditionalCreate's Null + Bool pairing is AWS's own published Deny
shape (conditional-writes-enforce.html Example 2); a review had suspected
it was vacuous, and it is not.
KNOWN CONSEQUENCES, documented rather than discovered later:
* CopyObject fails on this bucket (403 without the header, 501 with it) --
an accepted cost, since nothing copies journal objects.
* A PutObject with NO object-lock-mode header SUCCEEDS, inheriting the
bucket's 28-day COMPLIANCE default. That is a protected write, not an
unlocked one; the live probe verified the resulting retention.
* The bucket-owner ROOT principal can still replace this policy (an
explicit S3 recovery exception). Existing COMPLIANCE locks survive it.
